entry.title: [ai] Anthropic unveils Claude Mythos Preview, an AI that autonomously exploits zero-day vulnerabilities across every major OS
entry.summary: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview autonomously discovered and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser during internal testing, prompting the company to withhold public release and launch Project Glasswing, a controlled-access defensive coalition of approximately 40 organizations.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview autonomously discovered and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser during internal testing, prompting the company to withhold public release and launch Project Glasswing, a controlled-access defensive coalition of approximately 40 organizations.

Claude Mythos Preview was announced April 7, 2026, as Anthropic's most capable general-purpose model to date, with exceptional capability on computer security tasks. During internal evaluation, Mythos fully autonomously identified and exploited a 17-year-old FreeBSD NFS remote code execution vulnerability allowing unauthenticated root access—with no human involvement after the initial request. On Firefox JavaScript exploits, the previous model (Opus 4.6) succeeded 2 times in several hundred attempts; Mythos succeeded 181 times, roughly a 90-fold improvement. Mythos also constructed sophisticated multi-stage attacks including JIT heap sprays and privilege escalation chains that would take human experts weeks to build. Project Glasswing, launched simultaneously, gives approximately 40 partner organizations including AWS, Apple, Microsoft, Google, CrowdStrike, and Palo Alto Networks access to Mythos for coordinated defensive vulnerability disclosure. Anthropic commits to 90-day coordinated disclosure timelines, but fewer than 1 percent of Mythos-discovered vulnerabilities have been patched to date, indicating an enormous backlog of critical unresolved flaws.

Why it matters: The gap between Mythos's offensive capability and current defensive patch rates is the key danger signal: the lab itself acknowledges that fewer than 1 percent of discovered vulnerabilities have been remediated, meaning the model has effectively mapped a vast attack surface that humanity cannot currently defend at speed. CEO Dario Amodei has publicly characterized this as a 'narrow window' for tech firms, governments, and banks to fix vulnerabilities before adversaries independently develop comparable AI offensive tools. The decision to restrict Mythos rather than release publicly represents a significant departure from Anthropic's prior approach, and the Glasswing model—controlled access with coordinated disclosure requirements—may become the template for managing dual-use AI capabilities across the industry. The EU AI Act's general-purpose AI provisions include systemic-risk obligations for models like Mythos, and the case tests whether voluntary self-governance by a frontier lab is a sufficient compliance posture. Every AI lab is watching: if Glasswing successfully hardens critical infrastructure before the model's capabilities are replicated elsewhere, it demonstrates a viable path between full suppression and unrestricted deployment.

entry.title: [global politics] Iran drone strikes target Qatar, UAE, and Kuwait on May 10, testing the fragile US-brokered ceasefire
entry.summary: Iran launched drone attacks against a cargo vessel off Qatar, military sites in the UAE and Kuwait on May 10, threatening the month-old ceasefire and sending shockwaves through Gulf states that host major US military bases.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran launched drone attacks against a cargo vessel off Qatar, military sites in the UAE and Kuwait on May 10, threatening the month-old ceasefire and sending shockwaves through Gulf states that host major US military bases.

On Sunday May 10, a drone struck a commercial cargo vessel 23 nautical miles northeast of Doha in Qatari waters, igniting a small fire that was extinguished with no casualties; the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre confirmed the incident. The UAE Defense Ministry announced that two Iranian drones were shot down, directly attributing the attack to Tehran. Kuwait's Defense Ministry reported intercepting multiple hostile drones in Kuwaiti airspace in the early hours, dealing with them 'in accordance with established procedures.' The ceasefire has nominally been in effect since April 8, 2026, but both sides exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on May 8; Iran's IRGC Navy had warned that any attack on its tankers would trigger a 'heavy assault' on US regional bases. The attacks occurred on the same day Iran transmitted its formal ceasefire response via Pakistan, rejecting the US demand for a 12-year uranium enrichment moratorium and conditioning any deal on an end to all hostilities including on the Lebanon front. Iran holds approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent purity, per UN nuclear agency assessments.

Why it matters: Iran's simultaneous diplomatic submission and drone attacks on three Gulf states is a deliberate dual-track coercion strategy: negotiate with one hand, demonstrate military reach with the other, in order to extract better terms from Washington. The cargo ship strike in Qatari waters is the most escalatory element because Qatar hosts Al Udeid, the largest US air base in the Middle East, and a drone striking vessels in Qatari waters tests the boundary of direct threat to American forces. With Iran's counterproposal rejecting both the nuclear timeline and the sequencing of denuclearization before a ceasefire, the fundamental disagreement has hardened: Tehran insists on security guarantees before disarmament; Washington insists on disarmament before guarantees—a deadlock that has historically required years of diplomacy or a major military inflection to resolve. The Strait of Hormuz carries approximately 20 percent of global oil exports; continued ceasefire instability keeps energy markets volatile and tests allied cohesion among Gulf states, European NATO members dependent on Gulf energy, and the Trump administration's claim that the ceasefire remains 'in effect.' The next 48-72 hours of US and Gulf state diplomatic response will determine whether these attacks are treated as a ceasefire violation requiring action or are absorbed as negotiating background noise.

entry.title: [tech] Anthropic launches $1.5 billion enterprise AI services joint venture with Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, and Hellman & Friedman
entry.summary: Anthropic co-launched a $1.5 billion enterprise AI services joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, and Singapore's GIC to embed AI engineers inside mid-sized companies—community banks, regional manufacturers, and health systems—that lack the resources for sophisticated Claude deployments.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Anthropic co-launched a $1.5 billion enterprise AI services joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, and Singapore's GIC to embed AI engineers inside mid-sized companies—community banks, regional manufacturers, and health systems—that lack the resources for sophisticated Claude deployments.

The joint venture, announced May 4, 2026, is backed by a consortium including General Atlantic, Leonard Green, Apollo Global Management, GIC, and Sequoia Capital, with Anthropic, Blackstone, and Hellman & Friedman each contributing approximately $300 million. The new firm targets companies beneath the Fortune 500 threshold: health systems, community banks, regional manufacturers, and similar organizations that have not been served by Anthropic's existing partnerships with Accenture, Deloitte, and PwC. The business model is implementation-first: applied AI engineers from Anthropic work alongside the firm's own engineers to redesign client workflows and build custom Claude integrations, then provide long-term support—fundamentally different from a pure API access or consulting engagement. CFO Krishna Rao explained the rationale: 'Enterprise demand for Claude is significantly outpacing any single delivery model.' The announcement came the same day OpenAI announced a comparable joint venture, signaling that the two largest frontier AI labs have converged on the same go-to-market strategy for capturing mid-market enterprise revenue.

Why it matters: By bringing in Blackstone—the world's largest alternative asset manager with roughly $1 trillion in AUM and portfolio companies spanning healthcare, logistics, real estate, and infrastructure—and Goldman Sachs with relationships across thousands of corporate clients, Anthropic gains an instant distribution channel to exactly the mid-market customers it could not previously reach at scale. For incumbent management consulting and systems integration firms—Accenture, Deloitte, McKinsey's AI practice—this JV is a direct threat: it bundles model access, implementation, and long-term support under one roof at pricing middle-market budgets can sustain, compressing the margin on which consultants depend. The simultaneous OpenAI JV announcement suggests the frontier AI market is entering a deployment phase in which go-to-market and distribution advantages matter as much as model quality, and raises the question of whether mid-market companies will standardize on Claude or ChatGPT in ways that create durable switching costs. The healthcare use case highlighted in the announcement—redirecting physician time from documentation to patient care—is also the sector most directly regulated by HIPAA and state health-data privacy laws, ensuring that regulatory compliance infrastructure will be a key competitive differentiator for whichever enterprise AI firm penetrates health systems first.

entry.title: [tech] Anthropic seals multi-gigawatt Google and Broadcom TPU deal as run-rate revenue triples to $30 billion
entry.summary: Anthropic has signed a multi-gigawatt compute agreement with Google and Broadcom for next-generation TPU capacity coming online from 2027, as the company's run-rate revenue surpassed $30 billion—more than tripling from $9 billion in December 2025.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Anthropic has signed a multi-gigawatt compute agreement with Google and Broadcom for next-generation TPU capacity coming online from 2027, as the company's run-rate revenue surpassed $30 billion—more than tripling from $9 billion in December 2025.

The compute partnership locks in multi-gigawatt deployment of Google's next-generation TPUs and Broadcom's custom AI chips, with capacity scheduled to come online starting in 2027—the largest infrastructure commitment in Anthropic's history. CFO Krishna Rao described the deal as necessary to serve 'exponential growth,' noting that the number of business customers spending more than $1 million annually has doubled in less than two months, now exceeding 1,000. The revenue surge—from $9 billion at end-2025 to more than $30 billion run-rate in May 2026—represents one of the fastest growth trajectories in enterprise software history, outpacing Salesforce's peak growth and Snowflake's IPO-era ramp. The deal deepens an already substantial relationship: Google has committed up to $40 billion in investment in Anthropic, and Anthropic has committed to spending $200 billion on Google Cloud over five years. The compute will be located primarily in the United States, consistent with Anthropic's November 2025 commitment to American AI infrastructure, and complements existing agreements with AWS Trainium and NVIDIA GPU capacity.

Why it matters: Compute capacity measured in gigawatts—rather than the megawatt scale that defined cloud data centers a decade ago—signals that frontier AI training and inference now rank among the largest electricity consumers in the technology sector, with planning cycles that stretch years ahead and capital requirements that rival semiconductor fabs. By locking in Google TPU and Broadcom capacity now, Anthropic hedges against the GPU supply constraints that have periodically slowed training schedules across the industry; the diversification across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, and NVIDIA GPUs also gives the company operational resilience if any single platform underdelivers on performance or schedule. For Google Cloud, the deal creates a durable structural dependency: if Anthropic's enterprise JV (announced the same week) succeeds in making Claude the default AI layer for thousands of mid-market companies, Google Cloud becomes the preferred infrastructure for that entire segment, improving Google's competitive position against AWS and Azure. The scale of the financial relationship now binding Anthropic to Google—$40 billion investment plus $200 billion cloud spending commitment over five years—raises governance questions about whether Anthropic's independence as a safety-focused 'public benefit' company is compatible with being structurally reliant on a single hyperscaler investor.

entry.title: [tech law] Bambu Lab sends cease-and-desist to OrcaSlicer developer who restored cloud-printing feature company had disabled via firmware
entry.summary: Bambu Lab sent a cease-and-desist to Polish developer Pawel Jarczak after he published an OrcaSlicer fork restoring cloud-printing features the company had disabled via firmware in January 2025, raising unresolved questions about whether hardware manufacturers can weaponize AGPL copyright law to remove features from software they open-sourced.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Bambu Lab sent a cease-and-desist to Polish developer Pawel Jarczak after he published an OrcaSlicer fork restoring cloud-printing features the company had disabled via firmware in January 2025, raising unresolved questions about whether hardware manufacturers can weaponize AGPL copyright law to remove features from software they open-sourced.

In January 2025, Bambu Lab pushed firmware updates that severed OrcaSlicer's direct cloud-printing capability, forcing users to route connections through Bambu Connect, its proprietary bridge application. Developer Pawel Jarczak created OrcaSlicer-bambulab, a fork built on Bambu Studio's AGPL-3.0 licensed source code, to restore the disabled feature. Bambu Lab's cease-and-desist accused Jarczak of impersonating Bambu Studio, bypassing authorization controls, violating terms of use, reverse engineering proprietary software, and enabling modified clients to send 'arbitrary commands' to printers. Jarczak disputed each allegation, arguing his fork built exclusively on publicly available AGPL-3.0 code without redistributing any proprietary libraries—a license-compliance distinction he described as 'important.' Despite believing the accusations were legally unfounded, Jarczak voluntarily removed all releases from GitHub, citing inability to afford litigation costs. Right-to-repair advocate Louis Rossmann publicly offered to pay the first $10,000 of legal costs if Bambu Lab pursued formal action; users on Bambu Lab's own subreddit compared the company to 'the Nintendo of 3D printing.'

Why it matters: The Bambu Lab dispute crystallizes a legal gray area that has never been cleanly resolved in US courts: whether a hardware manufacturer can invoke DMCA Section 1201's anti-circumvention provisions or breach-of-contract theories to prevent owners of a physical device from using community software to communicate with that device over APIs the manufacturer controls. The AGPL-3.0 license requires source code disclosure and allows derivative works—Jarczak's core argument—but Bambu Lab's 'authorization controls' claim potentially invokes the DMCA's computer fraud provisions rather than pure copyright, a theory with broader chilling effect. Prior case law on printer cartridges (Lexmark) and garage door openers (Chamberlain) established that functional locking mechanisms can constitute DMCA violations, but courts have increasingly narrowed those rulings; the Bambu case would be the first major test in the context of open-source firmware and cloud APIs for consumer 3D printers. Right-to-repair laws enacted in California, New York, and the EU focus on physical repair access and spare parts—not software interoperability with connected devices—leaving this entire category legally exposed. The broader pattern—a company open-sources software to accelerate adoption, builds network effects and cloud dependency, then uses legal threats to suppress community features that undermine its subscription or data model—is a template being watched carefully by makers of connected hardware across consumer electronics, home automation, and industrial equipment.

entry.title: [law] SCOTUSblog: The 'two-three-four wild card court' and what Blanche v. Lau tells us about the new SCOTUS coalition dynamics
entry.summary: Legal analyst Rory Little's 'two-three-four wild card court' framework redraws the traditional 3-3-3 conservative/moderate/liberal model of the Supreme Court, identifying four justices—Roberts, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett—as genuinely unpredictable swing voters whose case-specific judgments now determine most outcomes.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Legal analyst Rory Little's 'two-three-four wild card court' framework redraws the traditional 3-3-3 conservative/moderate/liberal model of the Supreme Court, identifying four justices—Roberts, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett—as genuinely unpredictable swing voters whose case-specific judgments now determine most outcomes.

Little argues the Thomas-Alito bloc (solid 2) and the Sotomayor-Kagan-Jackson bloc (solid 3) are stable, but the four remaining justices—Roberts, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett—vote as swing votes rather than as a unified bloc, making coalition-building unpredictable case by case. The most surprising repositioning is Gorsuch: once assumed to be a reliable fifth conservative vote, Little places him as a wild card based on his textualism applied in ways that favor criminal defendants, immigrants, and Native American interests against government overreach—positions that have repeatedly aligned him with the liberal justices. The case Blanche v. Lau illustrates the model: Muk Choi Lau, a lawful permanent resident since 2007, was detained at JFK upon return from China when immigration officers found a felony trademark counterfeiting indictment in an FBI database; the Second Circuit ruled the government lacked 'clear and convincing evidence' at the time of reentry as required for normal-admission denial. The government appeals to SCOTUS, asking whether a pending felony indictment alone suffices for border officers to detain an LPR without satisfying the evidentiary standard. Little proposes a narrow holding—pending charges should suffice for preliminary parole pending removal proceedings—that could attract a supermajority while avoiding a broad proof-standard ruling.

Why it matters: The 2-3-4 wild card framework has immediate practical significance for lawyers and advocates: if four justices are genuinely unpredictable rather than two, the Supreme Court becomes harder to model strategically, which paradoxically makes in-person oral argument more influential—nuanced advocacy before potentially persuadable justices matters more than baseline vote-counting. For immigration law specifically, Blanche v. Lau asks a narrow but high-stakes question: whether LPRs returning after international travel can be detained based on criminal database hits without a full evidentiary hearing at the border, a question affecting hundreds of thousands of permanent residents who travel internationally. If the Court validates the government's position, it would effectively give border officers broad detention authority over LPRs with pending criminal charges regardless of the strength of the underlying case—expanding executive power in immigration enforcement at the border checkpoint before any judicial review. The case is also a test of how Gorsuch's textualism plays out in immigration law: the INA's 'at the time of' language is central, and Gorsuch's approach to statutory text could produce an outcome that surprises both immigration advocates and the Trump administration. A narrow ruling along the lines Little proposes—parole pending removal proceedings is acceptable even without full 'clear and convincing' proof—would give both sides a partial win and is the outcome most consistent with the 2-3-4 model.

entry.title: [global politics] Australia's One Nation wins historic first lower house seat in Farrer by-election, ending 77-year Coalition hold
entry.summary: Australia's far-right One Nation party won its first-ever seat in the House of Representatives on May 10, with candidate David Farley capturing 59.1 percent of the vote in the Farrer by-election and ending a 77-year Coalition hold on the rural New South Wales electorate.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Australia's far-right One Nation party won its first-ever seat in the House of Representatives on May 10, with candidate David Farley capturing 59.1 percent of the vote in the Farrer by-election and ending a 77-year Coalition hold on the rural New South Wales electorate.

The Farrer by-election was called after Sussan Ley, leader of the centre-right Liberal Party, resigned the seat in February 2026. Farley, a former agribusiness consultant, defeated independent Michelle Milthorpe with 59.1 percent to 40.8 percent of the vote in the sprawling southern New South Wales electorate, which covers agricultural and rural communities long dominated by the Nationals and Liberals. One Nation, founded by Senator Pauline Hanson in 1997, has held Senate seats and state legislature seats but has never previously won a federal lower house seat in its 30-year history—making Saturday's result a historic milestone. The win does not materially shift power in the lower house, where Labor holds 94 of 150 seats, but it marks a consolidation of far-right populist support in regional Australia that analysts have been tracking since One Nation's strong Senate performance in 2016. Farley ran on immigration restriction, domestic energy independence, and rural economic grievances—themes that resonate in an electorate with high fuel costs, declining agricultural margins, and skepticism of urban-driven climate policy.

Why it matters: One Nation's lower house breakthrough matters not because Farley's single seat changes the parliamentary arithmetic, but because it confirms that the 2016 Senate surge was not an aberration and that far-right populism has embedded itself structurally in Australian federal politics for the first time. The Farrer result fits a pattern visible in France (Le Pen's National Rally), Italy (Fratelli d'Italia), Hungary (Fidesz's right-wing consolidation), and now Australia—regional communities feeling economically marginalised and culturally threatened by urban policy priorities are shifting toward nationalist-populist parties that were previously viewed as protest vehicles rather than governing forces. For the Liberal-National Coalition, the result signals a serious challenge: Farrer was a safe Coalition seat for nearly eight decades, and its loss to One Nation rather than Labor or an independent suggests that the Coalition's rural base is fragmenting from the right, not just the center. The result also comes as Australia debates several policy questions—immigration levels, net-zero emissions targets, housing costs—where One Nation's positions have measurable public support in non-metropolitan areas, making the party a potential kingmaker in future minority government scenarios. The BBC and international media coverage of the result reflects growing attention to Australia as a test case for whether right-wing populism can achieve durable legislative presence in Westminster systems with compulsory voting.

entry.title: SpaceX Backs Anthropic with Colossus 1 Compute Access While Musk Simultaneously Sues OpenAI
entry.summary: SpaceX agreed to grant Anthropic access to its 220,000-GPU Colossus 1 data center in Memphis, Tennessee — providing 300 megawatts of new compute capacity within one month — while Elon Musk simultaneously pursues his lawsuit against OpenAI, making SpaceX a direct compute backer of OpenAI's most capable competitor.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

SpaceX agreed to grant Anthropic access to its 220,000-GPU Colossus 1 data center in Memphis, Tennessee — providing 300 megawatts of new compute capacity within one month — while Elon Musk simultaneously pursues his lawsuit against OpenAI, making SpaceX a direct compute backer of OpenAI's most capable competitor.

The deal gives Anthropic access to SpaceX's Colossus 1 facility in Memphis, housing more than 220,000 Nvidia processors with 300 megawatts of power capacity available within one month — enough electricity to power over 300,000 homes. Anthropic will use the compute to enhance Claude Pro and Claude Max assistants, and simultaneously announced it was doubling rate limits for paid plans, removing peak-hour usage caps, and increasing developer request volumes. The arrangement is strategically pointed: Musk is actively suing OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging OpenAI abandoned its nonprofit mission in favor of commercial interests, and SpaceX's simultaneous support of Anthropic — which competes directly with OpenAI — functions as a compute-level second front in that competitive conflict. Musk stated he approved the deal after meeting Anthropic's leadership, saying 'No one set off my evil detector.' Both parties expressed interest in eventually collaborating on 'multiple gigawatts of space-based orbital data centres,' tying the arrangement to SpaceX's broader IPO and orbital compute ambitions. Separately, Anthropic was excluded from a Pentagon classified-network AI deal that went to Microsoft, Google, and xAI.

Why it matters: Access to 220,000 Nvidia GPUs at a single facility is a training- and inference-scale resource that materially changes Anthropic's competitive position relative to OpenAI's Azure relationship and Google's TPU infrastructure, which had been the two dominant compute partnerships in frontier AI. The deal is partly a strategic Musk calculation: backing Anthropic with hardware while litigating against OpenAI functions as a market fragmentation move — Musk apparently prefers a frontier AI market with multiple competitive poles to one where OpenAI holds dominant position. For Anthropic, the benefit includes independence from sole reliance on Amazon Web Services as its primary compute partner, which reduces its negotiating constraints on pricing and priority access during peak demand. The orbital data center ambition is worth monitoring: if SpaceX's Starship-based orbital compute infrastructure materializes at gigawatt scale, it would give Anthropic access to compute outside terrestrial power grid constraints at a moment when US energy policy and data center permitting are becoming significant bottlenecks for frontier model training. The concurrent Pentagon exclusion creates a notable asymmetry in US AI policy: Anthropic, which has the most developed published safety frameworks among major frontier labs, holds no classified-network contracts, while competitors with fewer public safety commitments hold government AI relationships.

entry.title: DMA at Two: EU's Big Tech Law Produced Real Market Changes—but Compliance Theater Blunts Its Impact
entry.summary: Two years after the EU Digital Markets Act entered into force, analysis finds the regulation has produced tangible gains—a 500 million euro Apple fine, cross-platform messaging rights, measurable browser competition—but up to 66 percent of frequent users report that gatekeeper compliance increases friction rather than delivering the promised consumer benefits.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Two years after the EU Digital Markets Act entered into force, analysis finds the regulation has produced tangible gains—a 500 million euro Apple fine, cross-platform messaging rights, measurable browser competition—but up to 66 percent of frequent users report that gatekeeper compliance increases friction rather than delivering the promised consumer benefits.

The Digital Markets Act took effect in May 2023, designating seven platforms as "gatekeepers"—Apple, Google, Meta, Amazon, ByteDance, and two others—and imposing interoperability, data-sharing, and anti-steering obligations designed to open their ecosystems to competition. Concrete changes for EU consumers include the ability to set alternative browsers and payment apps as iPhone defaults, enforceable cross-platform messaging (a Latvian startup called BirdyChat now allows users to message WhatsApp contacts from outside Meta's ecosystem), and choice screens that have measurably shifted browser market share toward privacy-focused alternatives like Firefox. The Commission fined Apple 500 million euros in April 2025 for anti-steering violations that blocked App Store developers from directing users to cheaper purchases outside the App Store, and fined Meta 200 million euros for its "consent-or-pay" advertising model—both fines have been appealed. The Commission's April 2026 first formal DMA review declared the law "fit for purpose" while acknowledging a "ping-pong" enforcement dynamic: gatekeepers submit changes, the Commission requests improvements, and the cycle repeats without conclusive resolution. The Commission is now investigating Meta's integration of AI features into WhatsApp without a user opt-out, testing whether the DMA's systemic-risk provisions can reach AI-embedded features that post-date the regulation's drafting.

Why it matters: The DMA's two-year record reveals the gap between structural obligation and behavioral change: Apple and Meta have technically complied with most formal requirements while engineering compliance to increase friction and discourage users from exercising the rights the law creates—a pattern up to 66 percent of frequent users report experiencing as longer searches and less relevant results, and critics describe as "compliance theater." The 500 million euro Apple fine and 200 million euro Meta fine are significant but represent small fractions of both companies' annual revenues; credible deterrence requires the Commission to demonstrate willingness to escalate toward the DMA's ceiling of 10 percent of global annual turnover, a threshold that has not yet been invoked. The AI integration investigations are the most consequential test of the DMA's scope since enactment: if embedding AI features constitutes a new market-access barrier under Article 34 systemic-risk obligations, the regulation's reach will extend far beyond what the 2023 text explicitly anticipated and could require legislative clarification. The "fit for purpose" review signals no legislative revisions are imminent, meaning enforcement-through-fines remains the primary lever for at least two more years, making the size and sequencing of upcoming penalty decisions the decisive variable for the DMA's deterrence effect. Transatlantic tensions complicate enforcement: the Trump administration has signaled it views DMA actions targeting American companies as discriminatory trade policy, creating diplomatic pressure the Commission must navigate alongside its legal proceedings.

entry.title: What the EU AI Omnibus Deal Changes for the AI Act and What Lies Ahead
entry.summary: The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement on May 7 to amend the AI Act, delaying high-risk system compliance deadlines by over a year while adding a new ban on AI nudifier tools and broadening permissions to use sensitive personal data for bias detection.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement on May 7 to amend the AI Act, delaying high-risk system compliance deadlines by over a year while adding a new ban on AI nudifier tools and broadening permissions to use sensitive personal data for bias detection.

The Digital AI Omnibus package, finalized in early-morning negotiations in Brussels on May 7, 2026, extends the compliance deadline for standalone high-risk AI systems under Annex III — covering biometrics, law enforcement, border control, and critical infrastructure — from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, a 16-month extension. AI systems embedded in regulated products such as medical devices, machinery, and toys receive an even longer runway until August 2, 2028. The deal reflects sustained lobbying by European industry groups backed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who personally pressed for broader industrial exemptions and secured France and Italy's backing; Parliament ultimately limited exemptions to the machinery sector. Parliament's right wing prioritized industry relief; the left wing traded concessions to secure the new nudifier ban, which prohibits AI tools generating realistic non-consensual nude images and takes effect December 2026 — directly responding to millions of deepfake cases linked to Grok. Transparency and AI-generated content watermarking obligations under Article 50 retain the August 2 deadline, though existing deployed systems receive grace periods. SME privileges were extended to small mid-cap companies, and a new EU-level regulatory sandbox was established to allow controlled testing of high-risk AI.

Why it matters: The 16-month extension for high-risk AI removes the most immediate compliance pressure from companies developing AI for healthcare, law enforcement, and critical infrastructure — the sectors where certification requirements generated the greatest industry pushback, with compliance cost estimates running to tens of millions of euros per system. The delay is a direct concession to competitiveness arguments that the original August 2026 deadline would disadvantage European companies against US and Chinese competitors operating under lighter AI regulation. The nudifier ban is the deal's meaningful civil society win: placing an affirmative prohibition directly in the AI Act rather than relying solely on the Digital Services Act and criminal law creates a new EU-level enforcement vector against platforms hosting or generating such content. The Data Omnibus — the companion regulation addressing GDPR simplification — remains outstanding and poses greater risks, as it would broaden personal data processing permissions for AI training. The provisional agreement must receive formal approval from EU member states and the European Parliament, with Ireland taking over the Council presidency on June 30, timing that will determine how quickly formal adoption proceeds — and whether the August 2 transparency deadline triggers first compliance actions before high-risk rules take effect.

entry.title: Musk v. Altman Week 2: OpenAI Fires Back as Shivon Zilis Reveals Musk Tried to Recruit Altman to Tesla
entry.summary: As the $134 billion OpenAI trial entered its second week in Oakland, Shivon Zilis testified that Elon Musk attempted to recruit Sam Altman to lead a competing AI company at Tesla and asked researcher Andrej Karpathy to compile a list of top OpenAI employees to poach, while OpenAI countered that Musk is suing to destroy a commercial rival to xAI.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

FBI agents raided the Portsmouth home office of Virginia Democratic State Senate leader L. Louise Lucas—the legislator whose redistricting effort produced a 10-1 Democratic congressional advantage ratified by voters in April—with Fox News already positioned at the scene before the search began, raising questions about law enforcement-media coordination.

Louise Lucas was the central Democratic figure in Virginia's 2026 redistricting initiative, a Democrat-led effort to redraw the state's congressional district boundaries in response to prior Republican gerrymandering. Virginia voters approved the new maps via referendum in April 2026, shifting the congressional delegation from a 6-5 Democratic advantage to a projected 10-1 Democratic majority—a dramatic reversal that prompted Trump to label the outcome a "RIGGED ELECTION" on Truth Social and Lucas to respond to Senator Ted Cruz's criticism with "You all started it and we fucking finished it." Fox News reporter Alex Hogan—previously listed as a London-based correspondent—was already present at the search site before agents arrived; Fox subsequently revised Hogan's biography page after scrutiny of this fact emerged. As of publication, no charges have been filed against Lucas and no court documents have been made public.

Why it matters: The most significant legal question is whether the FBI's apparent pre-coordination with Fox News before an unannounced search raises Fourth Amendment execution concerns and whether the timing—against a legislator whose redistricting maps the administration publicly denounced—creates a pattern that implicates First Amendment and equal-protection principles even if the stated underlying allegations are formally unrelated to redistricting. Fox's advance knowledge suggests someone in or with access to the investigative chain informed the outlet, conduct that, if proven, could affect the admissibility of evidence and expose participants to accountability under DOJ leak guidelines. Virginia's redistricting fight is itself a downstream consequence of the Supreme Court's 2019 Rucho v. Common Cause decision that partisan gerrymandering is a non-justiciable political question; states have since engaged in an unregulated partisan mapmaking competition with no federal judicial check. The raid joins a growing pattern of federal law enforcement actions against Democratic officials involved in electoral map challenges, which civil rights organizations say raises systemic rule-of-law concerns regardless of individual cases' legal merits. Lucas's defiant public posture signals that any eventual charges will be contested aggressively and framed as politically motivated prosecution, making the government's charging decision—and its timing—a significant political and legal event in its own right.

entry.title: Too Dangerous to Deploy: Anthropic’s Mythos and What Comes Next
entry.summary: Anthropic’s Mythos Preview — a frontier AI model that can autonomously exploit software vulnerabilities within hours of discovery — is the first AI system deemed too dangerous for public release, spurring the Trump administration to reverse course on AI oversight.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Anthropic’s Mythos Preview — a frontier AI model that can autonomously exploit software vulnerabilities within hours of discovery — is the first AI system deemed too dangerous for public release, spurring the Trump administration to reverse course on AI oversight.

On April 7, 2026, Anthropic announced Mythos Preview, a frontier AI model with hacking capabilities so potent the company declared it “too dangerous” for unrestricted public release. Mythos can autonomously identify and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities “potentially within minutes or hours of discovery” — capabilities that “surpass all but the most skilled human” operators, according to Anthropic. The company reported the model had already found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, including some in every major operating system and web browser. Rather than a standard commercial launch, Anthropic restricted access to approximately 50 industry partners — including Amazon, Apple, Cisco, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA — through Project Glasswing, a defensive cybersecurity initiative backed by $100 million in usage credits and $4 million in direct donations to non-profit security groups. The Pentagon had designated Anthropic a “supply chain risk” in March 2026, but Mythos’s capabilities prompted Dario Amodei to meet White House officials; Trump told CNBC afterward that a defense deal was “possible.” The Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation subsequently announced expanded pre-deployment testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI.

Why it matters: Mythos marks the first instance of a major AI lab voluntarily restricting a commercial model’s release on capability-safety grounds rather than product readiness — a precedent the AI governance community has long advocated but never secured through voluntary commitments alone. The model’s autonomous vulnerability exploitation compresses the patch-response window from the current weeks-to-months standard to potentially hours, rendering current patch cadence fatally inadequate for under-resourced institutions like hospitals, schools, and utilities. The Trump administration’s shift from opposition to Biden-era AI oversight toward active model-testing frameworks signals that national security realities can override ideological hostility to regulation — but the resulting framework remains voluntary and fragmented, covering only companies that signed CAISI agreements. European allies were excluded from Glasswing’s 50 founding partners, intensifying transatlantic tensions over AI access and defensive coordination. The key question: whether Congress codifies any pre-deployment evaluation requirement, or whether Mythos remains a one-time exception that the next generation of AI companies is free to ignore.

entry.title: The Dialectic of Viewpoint Discrimination
entry.summary: On the anniversary of Germany’s World War II surrender, the Bundesrat began debate on a Hesse-sponsored bill that would criminalize publicly denying Israel’s right to exist with up to five years in prison, reigniting a fundamental constitutional debate about whether Germany’s historical obligations can justify viewpoint-based speech restrictions.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

On the anniversary of Germany’s World War II surrender, the Bundesrat began debate on a Hesse-sponsored bill that would criminalize publicly denying Israel’s right to exist with up to five years in prison, reigniting a fundamental constitutional debate about whether Germany’s historical obligations can justify viewpoint-based speech restrictions.

The proposed legislation, introduced by the state of Hesse in the Bundesrat, would create a new criminal offence targeting anyone who “publicly or in an assembly denies the right of the State of Israel to exist or calls for the elimination of the State of Israel in a manner capable of encouraging antisemitic acts of violence or arbitrary measures.” Hesse frames the bill as closing a legal loophole not covered by Holocaust denial laws, with penalties of up to five years in prison or a fine. The top administrative court in North Rhine-Westphalia ruled in November 2025 that questioning Israel’s right to exist does not constitute an existing criminal offence — exactly the gap the bill targets. A virtually identical Hesse proposal failed two years earlier after leading legal scholars and practitioners objected on constitutional grounds. The deliberate timing of the first Bundesrat reading on May 8, the anniversary of Germany’s unconditional surrender, reinforces the legislation’s framing as a response to Germany’s specific historical responsibility toward Jewish life.

Why it matters: The bill tests a structural tension in German constitutional law: the Basic Law’s Article 5 protections for free expression permit restrictions only through “general laws,” meaning the state cannot restrict speech based on its content or viewpoint. Criminal laws against Holocaust denial passed the “general law” test because courts found they targeted a narrow, historically specific deception rather than a political opinion; it is much less clear whether “denial of Israel’s right to exist” satisfies the same standard, because the concept is inherently political and contested. The earlier Hesse bill failed for precisely this reason: leading constitutional scholars argued it constituted viewpoint discrimination — the state criminalizing one side of a political dispute rather than banning incitement or deception as such. If enacted, the law is almost certain to reach the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), which would have to determine whether Germany’s heightened duty to protect Jewish life justifies content-based speech restrictions beyond Holocaust denial. The European Court of Human Rights has struck down analogous laws in other Council of Europe jurisdictions under Article 10, meaning a German statute of this kind would likely generate international litigation spanning both national and European courts simultaneously.

entry.title: Once Again, Trump Looks To Get Out Of Paying E. Jean Carroll By Having The DOJ Substitute In For Himself
entry.summary: The Trump Justice Department filed a Supreme Court motion invoking the Westfall Act to substitute the federal government as defendant in the E. Jean Carroll defamation case — a maneuver three courts have already rejected — which would extinguish Carroll’s $88.3 million verdict if the Court accepts it.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Trump Justice Department filed a Supreme Court motion invoking the Westfall Act to substitute the federal government as defendant in the E. Jean Carroll defamation case — a maneuver three courts have already rejected — which would extinguish Carroll’s $88.3 million verdict if the Court accepts it.

Trump faces $88.3 million in combined judgments from two Carroll jury verdicts: one for sexual abuse and a separate defamation award arising from Trump’s public denials of Carroll’s account. The Westfall Act allows the federal government to substitute itself as defendant when a government employee has acted within the scope of official duties; if substituted, the case would be dismissed because citizens cannot sue the government for defamation in the same manner. Three separate courts have rejected this argument: the Attorney General explicitly declined Westfall certification during the original 2023 district court proceedings, and courts ruled that waiver belongs to the United States as an entity — not to individual administrations that can revisit it; the 2025 attempt came post-trial and post-verdict, violating the statute’s procedural timing requirements; and courts found that “denying you raped someone is not part of the president’s official job.” A Second Circuit judge described the litigation as “deeply burdensome” while refusing en banc review of the substitution question for the third time. The matter now reaches the Supreme Court, which granted Trump broad presidential immunity in its 2024 Trump v. United States ruling.

Why it matters: The 2024 Trump v. United States immunity decision created the legal environment in which this renewed Westfall argument becomes more plausible — the Court has demonstrated willingness to expand the scope of what constitutes official presidential conduct, and the same logic could theoretically extend to statements made during or about a president’s tenure. If the Court accepts the substitution, it would allow any president to escape personal civil liability by retrospectively invoking government immunity, extinguishing jury verdicts that have already been rendered after full trial. The procedural irregularity matters: the DOJ’s willingness to re-argue a question courts have ruled waived suggests the government is treating successive administrations as separate legal actors who can relitigate finalized procedural decisions — a theory with significant implications for civil litigation involving government officials. Carroll would be left with an uncollectible verdict despite prevailing twice before juries, setting a precedent that future presidential defendants could exploit to run out the clock on civil accountability. The case is now a direct test of whether the Court’s 2024 immunity expansion extends into civil defamation law, a domain where First Amendment doctrine has previously treated presidential speech about public controversies as a matter of free expression rather than sovereign immunity.

entry.title: What I learned attending all those Supreme Court oral arguments this term
entry.summary: SCOTUSblog’s Amy Howe attended nearly every oral argument in the 2025-26 term and found a court under visible internal strain, with sessions running nearly double their scheduled length, justices speaking simultaneously in “face-offs,” and public inter-justice conflicts spilling from courtroom into speeches and social media.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

SCOTUSblog’s Amy Howe attended nearly every oral argument in the 2025-26 term and found a court under visible internal strain, with sessions running nearly double their scheduled length, justices speaking simultaneously in “face-offs,” and public inter-justice conflicts spilling from courtroom into speeches and social media.

Oral arguments in the 2025-26 term have nearly doubled their scheduled duration, a trend Howe attributes to multiplying advocates, more complex cases, and justices reluctant to cede question time; Chief Justice Roberts has indicated he may revise the format this summer. Multiple justices now regularly speak simultaneously — Howe calls these “face-offs” — with junior justices expected by unwritten protocol to yield to senior colleagues, and Roberts occasionally intervening when overlap becomes unmanageable. Attending arguments in person revealed dynamics invisible through livestream audio: Justice Amy Coney Barrett physically waved off Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson’s attempted interruption, and President Trump’s attendance at the birthright citizenship argument — the first sitting president present at any oral argument — visibly changed the courtroom’s tone. Women comprised only 30 percent of arguing lawyers in 2025-26, barely improved from 28 percent in 2016-17, and just 27 percent of Solicitor General’s office advocates — a striking gap given that office’s role in launching Supreme Court bar careers. Justice Samuel Alito expressed concern that arguments “can go on and on and on,” and in April’s session only one non-government lawyer argued before the Court for the first time among non-government counsel.

Why it matters: The practical effect of longer arguments is not more information for the justices — who have already read full briefing — but rather heightened fatigue and diminished engagement during second arguments in the same session, a dynamic Howe documents explicitly as visible from the courtroom. The public inter-justice conflicts from April 2026 — Justice Sotomayor’s speech about Kavanaugh, Justice Jackson’s Yale lecture criticizing shadow-docket orders, Justice Thomas’s public response — are reflected in the in-person dynamics: a bench that visibly argues with itself and projects internal divisions that once would have stayed behind closed conference-room doors. The concentration of the Supreme Court bar — with nearly all non-government arguing slots held by repeat advocates — raises access-to-justice concerns, since success in the increasingly extended, contentious format requires a level of preparation and institutional knowledge available to only a small group of practitioners. A format revision this summer could significantly alter oral argument as a legal institution: reducing time limits, restricting interruptions, or changing advocate selection rules would affect not only courtroom experience but also the signals the Court sends about how much it values live advocacy versus written briefs. Any structural change would also affect how the inter-justice tensions currently playing out in speeches might instead express themselves within the argument itself.

entry.summary: The Musk v. Altman trial, in which Elon Musk seeks Sam Altman’s removal and demands OpenAI revert to its nonprofit structure, raises fundamental questions about whether charitable mission statements embedded in AI company charters create enforceable legal obligations that override subsequent commercial restructuring.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Musk v. Altman trial, in which Elon Musk seeks Sam Altman’s removal and demands OpenAI revert to its nonprofit structure, raises fundamental questions about whether charitable mission statements embedded in AI company charters create enforceable legal obligations that override subsequent commercial restructuring.

The trial centers on OpenAI’s conversion from a nonprofit to a capped-profit company and its subsequent plans for a full for-profit restructuring, which Musk alleges abandons the founding mission to develop AI “for the benefit of humanity.” Evidence introduced during the trial shows OpenAI had fallen from second to near-last among major AI companies on the 2025 Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index; the company announced plans to introduce advertising into ChatGPT in January 2026 and disbanded its alignment team in February 2026 despite repeated lawsuits alleging premature model releases. Shivon Zilis — mother of Musk’s children and a former OpenAI board observer — testified that Musk had attempted to recruit Sam Altman to Tesla’s board before their falling-out, complicating Musk’s claim that his motives are purely mission-driven. The Verfassungsblog analysis by Teodora Groza, published May 8, argues the trial highlights a gap in European AI regulation: the EU AI Act sets technical safety requirements for AI systems but creates no enforceable governance standards for the AI organizations that build and deploy them. Groza identifies mandatory internal safety boards with independent experts, regulator-appointed observers embedded in AI organizations, and golden shares giving public authorities a direct governance stake as the structural instruments necessary to fill that gap.

Why it matters: The trial is the first judicial examination of whether a charitable mission embedded in a tech company’s founding documents creates legally binding constraints that override subsequent commercial restructuring decisions — a question with direct relevance to every AI company that has incorporated public-benefit language in its charter, safety commitments in its documentation, or mission-driven representations to regulators and investors. If a California court rules that OpenAI’s founding mission creates enforceable governance obligations, the precedent would affect not only OpenAI but every US benefit corporation and AI lab that has made comparable representations. From the EU’s perspective, the trial illustrates why the AI Act’s technical risk classification system is structurally insufficient: it can regulate what an AI system does technically, but it cannot govern who decides whether, when, and at what safety threshold that system is deployed commercially. Groza’s call for mandatory governance instruments — internal safety boards, regulator-appointed observers, golden shares — goes well beyond anything in current EU or US law, and it is unlikely to reach the EU’s AI Act implementing regulations before 2027 at the earliest. The case to watch after the verdict: whether any state attorney general intervenes to enforce charitable trust obligations against OpenAI’s restructuring, which is the most likely domestic enforcement mechanism even if Musk loses.

entry.title: Eighth Circuit Kills FCC's Digital Discrimination Rule, Eliminating Federal Oversight of Racial Broadband Gaps
entry.summary: The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously vacated the Biden FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule on May 8, holding the Commission exceeded its statutory authority by imposing disparate-impact liability on broadband providers — eliminating the only federal mechanism for addressing documented racial and economic gaps in internet infrastructure deployment.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously vacated the Biden FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule on May 8, holding the Commission exceeded its statutory authority by imposing disparate-impact liability on broadband providers — eliminating the only federal mechanism for addressing documented racial and economic gaps in internet infrastructure deployment.

The FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule, one of the final major Biden-era communications policy actions, created a complaint system under which consumers could challenge broadband deployment that produced racially or economically disparate outcomes, even without proving intentional discrimination. The rule applied not only to ISPs but also to their subcontractors and suppliers. A three-judge panel of the Eighth Circuit, composed of Republican-appointed judges, ruled unanimously that the FCC lacked authority to impose disparate-impact liability — the legal standard under which a facially neutral practice can violate anti-discrimination law if it produces disproportionately harmful outcomes without any showing of discriminatory intent. The court also struck the rule's extension to subcontractors as exceeding the agency's scope. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, praised the ruling; consumer advocacy groups including Public Knowledge criticized it as leaving documented infrastructure gaps in low-income and minority communities without any legal remedy at the federal level.

Why it matters: The Eighth Circuit's ruling leaves intentional discrimination as the only actionable federal standard for broadband equity enforcement — a bar that the analysis notes 'almost never exists in writing,' making successful enforcement practically impossible. Research consistently documents that high-speed infrastructure is less likely to be deployed in predominantly Black, Hispanic, and low-income communities; the rule was designed to address this pattern through the same disparate-impact framework governing housing and employment discrimination. With the rule vacated, affected communities are left to pursue patchwork state-level remedies or antitrust claims, both of which face higher evidentiary thresholds and lack the FCC's nationwide jurisdiction. The ruling fits a broader pattern in which federal courts have used major-questions doctrine and nondelegation reasoning to constrain agency authority under Biden-era regulations — a trend that has affected the FTC, EPA, NLRB, and now the FCC in rapid succession. States like California and New York with their own broadband anti-discrimination rules are the primary remaining enforcement actors, but their jurisdictions are bounded and their resources far smaller than a federal regulator's, meaning systematic national enforcement gaps are now essentially permanent absent congressional action.

entry.title: Court to DOGE: Asking ChatGPT 'Is This DEI?' Is Not Proper Legal Process and Also a First Amendment Violation
entry.summary: A federal judge issued a 143-page ruling on May 8 finding that DOGE staffers violated federal law and the First Amendment by terminating $163 million in National Endowment for the Humanities grants based solely on ChatGPT responses to 'Does this relate to DEI?' — without statutory authority, reasoned analysis, or any definition of the term they fed the chatbot.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A federal judge issued a 143-page ruling on May 8 finding that DOGE staffers violated federal law and the First Amendment by terminating $163 million in National Endowment for the Humanities grants based solely on ChatGPT responses to 'Does this relate to DEI?' — without statutory authority, reasoned analysis, or any definition of the term they fed the chatbot.

DOGE staffers Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh, described as having minimal relevant experience, reviewed National Endowment for the Humanities grants by copy-pasting summaries into ChatGPT and asking 'Does the following relate at all to DEI?' Judge Colleen McMahon of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York found the process void on three independent grounds. First, DOGE lacked statutory authority: Congress vested termination power in the NEH Chairperson alone, and the staffers had usurped decision-making authority, drafting termination letters under the Chair's name and overriding his recommendations. Second, the process was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act: Fox testified he never defined 'DEI' for the chatbot, and the resulting terminations flagged a study of ancient Jewish texts as DEI-related and rejected a human rights study documenting Uyghur persecution in China on the same grounds. Third, the terminations constituted viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment: the government admitted it was eliminating grants promoting a disfavored ideology, and the court stated plainly that 'DEI is, of course, a viewpoint.' The case was brought by the American Council of Learned Societies.

Why it matters: The ruling articulates what may be the most precise judicial statement on DOGE's structural constitutional limits: executive-branch advisory bodies cannot exercise decision-making authority Congress never delegated to them, and AI-tool outputs cannot substitute for the reasoned analysis the APA requires. The First Amendment holding is significant because it applies to grant administration — an area courts sometimes treat as executive discretion — establishing that the government cannot condition NEH grants on viewpoint conformity. The arbitrary-and-capricious analysis creates a reproducible legal template: any federal agency whose decisions were influenced by DOGE staffers lacking statutory authority faces identical APA challenges, and the ChatGPT methodology makes those challenges especially easy to document through agency records requests. DOGE has terminated billions of dollars in grants across multiple agencies using similar review processes, and this ruling directly raises the viability of parallel suits challenging those terminations nationwide. The decision also opens a broader debate about government use of AI tools in regulatory and enforcement contexts — whether AI-assisted screening can ever satisfy the APA's requirement for reasoned decision-making, and what level of documentation such processes require to withstand judicial review.

entry.title: But First, Implementation
entry.summary: Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party won a constitutional supermajority with 53% of the vote on May 9, demanded that President Tamás Sulyok and Chief Justice András Varga resign by May 31 or face removal, launching Hungary’s most consequential attempt at constitutional repair since Orbán’s 2010 consolidation.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party won a constitutional supermajority with 53% of the vote on May 9, demanded that President Tamás Sulyok and Chief Justice András Varga resign by May 31 or face removal, launching Hungary’s most consequential attempt at constitutional repair since Orbán’s 2010 consolidation.

Hungary’s 2026 parliamentary election saw Magyar’s Tisza party secure 53.1 percent of the vote, which under Hungary’s electoral system translated into a constitutional supermajority — enough seats to amend the constitution without coalition partners. Magyar was sworn in as prime minister in early May 2026, ending Viktor Orbán’s rule that began with a similar supermajority in 2010 and progressively restructured Hungary’s judiciary, prosecutorial service, and public broadcasting to entrench Fidesz authority. In his inaugural speech to the National Assembly, Magyar demanded President Tamás Sulyok — a Fidesz appointee — resign no later than May 31, and separately called on Chief Justice András Varga to do the same, calling both “puppets” of Orbán. Verfassungsblog’s analysis of the situation notes a central paradox: Tisza holds enough power to fix the constitution, but reversing Orbán’s changes while respecting European rule-of-law norms requires Magyar not to use the same majoritarian tools Orbán deployed. Hungary’s Constitutional Court, the Prosecutor General’s office, and the State Audit Office remain staffed by Fidesz-era appointees with fixed terms that cannot be easily shortened without constitutional changes Magyar has not yet formally proposed.

Why it matters: Hungary’s case is the sharpest live test of whether a post-autocratic government can dismantle illiberal institutions without replicating the constitutional shortcuts that built them — the same challenge Poland faced after its 2023 election, where the new government’s attempts to restore judicial independence triggered counter-challenges at the Constitutional Tribunal it was trying to reform. If Magyar removes Sulyok and Varga unilaterally, he risks creating the same type of executive-over-judiciary precedent that EU institutions condemned Orbán for establishing. If he waits for voluntary resignations that may never come, Fidesz-appointed officials retain enough institutional leverage — especially in the Constitutional Court — to block or delay his reform agenda. The EU’s rule-of-law conditionality framework, which froze approximately €30 billion in cohesion funds to Hungary during the Orbán era, is now watching whether Magyar’s government satisfies European Court of Justice standards in process as well as outcome. The May 31 deadline Magyar set is the first concrete test: Sulyok and Varga’s responses will signal whether the institutional transition will be negotiated or contested.

entry.title: When Justices Turn on Each Other
entry.summary: In an unusual cluster of public conflicts across three weeks in April 2026, Supreme Court justices criticized each other’s reasoning and character in speeches and writings, reflecting deep institutional tensions over emergency shadow-docket orders and the Trump administration’s aggressive use of executive power.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

In an unusual cluster of public conflicts across three weeks in April 2026, Supreme Court justices criticized each other’s reasoning and character in speeches and writings, reflecting deep institutional tensions over emergency shadow-docket orders and the Trump administration’s aggressive use of executive power.

Three separate incidents within an eight-day window in April 2026 crystallized growing public dysfunction at the Supreme Court. Justice Sonia Sotomayor criticized Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s solo concurrence in Noem v. Perdomo — an immigration enforcement case — during a University of Kansas Law School appearance on April 7, suggesting Kavanaugh lacked working-class empathy; she later issued a formal apology calling her remarks “inappropriate” and “hurtful.” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in a Yale Law School lecture on April 13, characterized approximately two dozen emergency docket orders favoring Trump administration positions as “scratch-paper musings” that “can seem oblivious and thus ring hollow,” directly targeting conservative colleagues’ reasoning. Justice Clarence Thomas responded on April 15 by lamenting that he had joined a court that no longer “dealt with differences as friends,” and criticizing colleagues who recast themselves as “institutionalists” or “thoughtful moderates.” Justice Elena Kagan separately warned that the emergency shadow docket was “never” designed to be used to circumvent established precedent such as Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935).

Why it matters: Public inter-justice disagreements of this intensity are historically rare and reflect genuine institutional stress, not mere judicial temperament. The structural root cause is the emergency shadow docket: it allows the court to issue consequential orders without full briefing or reasoned opinions, which strips dissenting justices of their normal vehicle for public disagreement — a written dissent — and forces them into speeches and media appearances instead. The volume of Trump administration emergency applications has made this a routine dynamic, with major executive-branch actions on firing agency heads, immigration enforcement, and foreign affairs being governed by shadow-docket orders that provide almost no precedent for lower courts to apply. Sotomayor’s apology is itself significant: she felt the institutional cost of being seen as attacking a colleague personally rather than legally, suggesting that even the most vocal critics recognize the reputational risk. The practical legal consequence is a court whose most important emergency decisions lack the reasoned analysis that would make them useful legal authority; what to watch is whether the court uses Noem v. Perdomo or a successor case to establish clearer emergency docket standards — the only structural fix available short of congressional action.

entry.title: Iran Accuses US of 'Reckless Military Adventure' as Hormuz Fire Exchange Strains Ceasefire
entry.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US on May 9 of choosing a 'reckless military adventure' over diplomacy after US forces disabled two Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving ten Iranian sailors wounded and five missing — escalating a standoff that Trump insists still constitutes a ceasefire but which each side is accusing the other of violating.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US on May 9 of choosing a 'reckless military adventure' over diplomacy after US forces disabled two Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving ten Iranian sailors wounded and five missing — escalating a standoff that Trump insists still constitutes a ceasefire but which each side is accusing the other of violating.

US forces fired on and disabled two Iranian oil tankers on May 8 after they allegedly attempted to bypass the American blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving 10 sailors wounded and 5 missing according to Iranian state media. This followed a May 7 exchange of fire in which Iran fired missiles and drones at three US Navy destroyers transiting the strait — the US called the attacks 'unprovoked' and said it responded in self-defense, while Iran claimed the US had violated the ceasefire by targeting an Iranian tanker first. The month-old ceasefire framework, established after US military strikes on Iran in April 2026, calls for a halt to hostilities, reopening of the Strait, and a 15–20 day negotiation window to address nuclear issues, freedom of navigation, and sanctions; Pakistan is mediating the diplomatic talks. On May 6, President Trump had paused operations described as 'Project Freedom' citing 'great progress' toward a possible agreement, but subsequent strikes have continued. Trump has maintained the ceasefire is still in effect, calling the strikes 'just a love tap.' Foreign Minister Araghchi stated that Iran would 'never bow to pressure' and accused Washington of triggering military escalation 'every time a diplomatic solution is on the table.'

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz carries approximately 20% of global oil trade, and each exchange of fire carries escalation risk that could trigger supply disruption and oil price spikes — energy markets are already pricing in a conflict premium from the ongoing crisis. Araghchi's 'reckless military adventure' framing signals that Iran may be positioning itself to formally declare the ceasefire void, which would restore full belligerency and eliminate the diplomatic pathway currently under Pakistani mediation. The symmetrical accusation dynamic — each side firing while calling the other's action a ceasefire violation — mirrors the early escalation sequence that preceded the initial US-Iran exchanges in March 2026 and suggests the ceasefire architecture lacks a neutral monitoring mechanism capable of distinguishing defensive from offensive actions. Pakistan's mediating role is the critical off-ramp: Iran is reviewing a US proposal covering nuclear rollback, navigation rights, and sanctions relief, and Araghchi's public condemnation sets up domestic political cover for rejecting it without formal negotiating blame. The US decision to disable additional tankers while awaiting an Iranian diplomatic response is a coercive diplomacy tactic with historically poor outcomes — simultaneous military pressure and diplomatic negotiation typically hardens the target's domestic political constraints rather than accelerating concessions.

entry.title: Putin Denounces NATO at Scaled-Back Victory Day Parade Featuring North Korean Troops
entry.summary: Russia held its most scaled-back Victory Day parade in nearly two decades on May 9 — no tanks or heavy weapons appeared for the first time since 2004 — while Putin declared Russia is fighting an 'aggressive force armed by all of NATO' and North Korean troops marched in Red Square for the first time, publicly confirming a bilateral military partnership Moscow had previously downplayed.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Russia held its most scaled-back Victory Day parade in nearly two decades on May 9 — no tanks or heavy weapons appeared for the first time since 2004 — while Putin declared Russia is fighting an 'aggressive force armed by all of NATO' and North Korean troops marched in Red Square for the first time, publicly confirming a bilateral military partnership Moscow had previously downplayed.

The 45-minute parade in Moscow's Red Square stripped all heavy military hardware — tanks, missiles, and armored vehicles that are the traditional centerpiece of the annual World War II commemoration were absent for the first time since the early Putin years, replaced by a video screen displaying equipment deployed to Ukraine. Russian officials attributed the reduced format to the 'current operational situation' and Ukrainian drone attack threats; authorities restricted all mobile internet and SMS in Moscow during the event. In his speech, Putin described Russia's war in Ukraine as 'just' and said soldiers were confronting 'an aggressive force armed and supported by the entire NATO bloc' — framing the conflict as civilizational defense against Western aggression rather than a territorial dispute. North Korean soldiers marched in the parade for the first time, credited by Russian authorities with 'contributions in the Kursk region,' an open acknowledgment of the estimated 10,000–12,000 North Korean troops that reporting indicates fought alongside Russian forces. Foreign dignitaries present were limited to leaders from close Russian allies including Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Laos, Malaysia, and Slovakia. A US-brokered three-day ceasefire covering May 10–12 had been announced, which Russian officials cited as reducing the risk of Ukrainian drone strikes on Moscow.

Why it matters: The absence of heavy military hardware from Victory Day for the first time in nearly 20 years is a significant intelligence signal: frontline commitments are severe enough that Russia could not safely pull adequate numbers of tanks and armored vehicles back to Moscow for a parade without operational impact, revealing the depth of materiel attrition after three years of high-intensity warfare. The open display of North Korean troops represents a formal change in Russia's diplomatic posture — Moscow had previously minimized or denied North Korean military involvement despite extensive documentation, and marching them in a military parade forecloses further deniability and signals Russia considers the Pyongyang alliance a strategic asset worth advertising to domestic and international audiences. The NATO framing of Putin's speech — characterizing Ukrainian defenders as mere proxies of the entire Alliance — reinforces a diplomatic posture that complicates ceasefire negotiations: any settlement requires Putin to claim some form of victory against 'NATO,' not merely Ukraine, raising the political cost for Moscow of accepting terms short of its maximalist goals. The concurrent US-brokered Ukraine ceasefire window (May 10–12) is the immediate diplomatic test: whether both sides observe it will determine whether the ceasefire architecture can be expanded into a more durable framework or whether the conflict resumes full intensity after the commemorative period ends.

entry.title: Péter Magyar Sworn in as Hungary’s Prime Minister, Ending Orbán’s 16-Year Rule
entry.summary: Péter Magyar took his oath of office as Hungary’s prime minister on May 9, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule, after his centre-right Tisza party won 141 of 199 parliamentary seats in April’s election on a platform of democratic restoration and EU reengagement.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Péter Magyar took his oath of office as Hungary’s prime minister on May 9, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule, after his centre-right Tisza party won 141 of 199 parliamentary seats in April’s election on a platform of democratic restoration and EU reengagement.

Magyar, 45, was sworn in at Hungary’s parliament on the morning of May 9, 2026, with Orbán absent from the inaugural session — a pointed absence by a leader who governed Hungary as what critics called an “illiberal democracy” since 2010. The Tisza party’s 141-seat majority in the 199-seat parliament gives Magyar the constitutional capacity to reverse much of Orbán’s institutional reshaping without requiring coalition partners. The EU flag was reinstalled on the parliament building on the same day, absent for approximately 12 years. Magyar entered politics in 2024 after his divorce from Orbán’s justice minister, gaining national attention by releasing leaked recordings exposing alleged Orbán-era corruption; he rose rapidly through civil society organizing before founding the Tisza party. Hungary experienced prolonged economic stagnation under Orbán — declining real wages, high inflation, and a significant exodus of educated citizens to Western Europe — which energized Magyar’s change platform. He has vowed to restore judicial independence, electoral integrity, and media pluralism, and to clamp down on alleged corruption within the previous government.

Why it matters: Magyar’s election is the most significant democratic transition in Central Europe since the post-communist era and directly alters the EU’s internal political dynamics. Orbán’s Hungary was the most consistent disruptor of EU consensus — blocking Ukraine aid packages, delaying NATO enlargement votes, and maintaining close ties with Putin while the rest of the EU imposed sanctions. A pro-EU majority in Budapest removes the single most reliable veto player from EU Council decision-making and could unlock billions in EU cohesion and recovery funds that Brussels had withheld over rule-of-law concerns. The judicial and constitutional repairs Magyar has promised — restoring independence of courts, electoral commissioners, and public media regulators — will take years and face likely resistance from Orbán-era appointees with fixed-term mandates that cannot be immediately terminated. The EU will need to decide how quickly to restore suspended funds: too fast rewards change symbolically before institutional reform is measurably implemented; too slow creates political difficulties for Magyar’s domestic reform agenda. The precedent matters for other EU member states where democratic backsliding is ongoing — the Hungary case demonstrates that electoral accountability can displace entrenched illiberal governments even without EU enforcement action succeeding.

entry.title: UK Warship HMS Dragon Heads to Middle East for Potential Strait of Hormuz Mission
entry.summary: Britain deployed the Type-45 destroyer HMS Dragon to the Middle East on May 9 as part of a UK-France jointly led multinational pre-positioning for a future Strait of Hormuz escort mission — the world’s most consequential oil shipping lane, effectively blocked since Iran shuttered it on February 28, 2026.
entry.content:
